🦠 New #Publication in Nature Communications (Nature Portfolio) —
𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐢𝐬 𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐡𝐮𝐛 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐧𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐛𝐢𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭, 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐬𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐚𝐬 𝐂-𝐂𝐀𝐌𝐏. These new antibiotics have the greatest impact potential in India and other Asian countries, as these nations face a very high AMR burden.

🔗 Read the paper here: https://lnkd.in/dUwXAsAv

This publication has been co-authored by Dr. Taslimarif Saiyed, PhD, Dir-CEO Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) | Abi Manesh, Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore | Kamini Walia, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) | Balaji Veeraraghavan, Christian Medical College (CMC), Vellore; and David Paterson, National University of Singapore

The paper features two antibiotic agents — BWC0977 and Klebicin by C-CAMP startups Bugworks Research Inc. and GangaGen Biotechnologies, respectively. Both agents are in Phase I and advanced pre-clinical stages of trials. The article also features two new antibiotic agents in early development, developed by Venus Remedies Limited, a partner of the C-CAMP-anchored India AMR Innovation Hub #IAIH. 

Additionally, the authors have listed antibiotics that have been developed and recently approved in India, along with multiple made-in-India antibiotics that are in Phase 2 trials and beyond. These antibiotic agents target Complicated Urinary Tract Infections #cUTI, Hospital Acquired Pneumonia #HAP, Ventilator Associated Pneumonia #VAP, Community Acquired Pneumonia #CAP.

This article focuses on antibiotic development in India and a path to equitable access across India. It further discusses how the country is gearing up to be a global hub for the development of novel antibiotics, conducting world-class regulatory-grade trials, and manufacturing.

Work in Progress, our monthly newsletter, now reaches close to 30,000 subscribers by email. More than 12,000 people subscribe to it here on LinkedIn, and that number is still climbing.

We chose the name in 2021, and it was not a marketing decision. It was an admission. We did not know how to build markets for innovations that had no business case yet. Five years on, we still do not know entirely. So we publish what we are learning: how our portfolio companies are building and de-risking, how end users and communities are adopting these solutions, and how the ecosystem is evolving.

The appetite for substance is far larger than that, and we have been underestimating our own audience for years. Some subscribers send us feedback. Some write back with corrections, which is the highest form of readership.

Our writing travels only as far as our readers carry it, and the people who most need to read about social impact, entrepreneurship, deep science and patient capital are usually outside our own echo chamber. Please subscribe, read and repost. That means a lot to us.

Social Alpha is still a work in progress. That remains the point.

Delighted to share the successful completion of the "City Camp – Essentials of Scientific Entrepreneurship," a two-day workshop organised by Venture Center and Tamil Nadu Veterinary and Animal Sciences University (TANUVAS) with CSR support from Kemin Industries.

The workshop brought together 130+ participants, including students, startups, aspiring entrepreneurs and innovators, for two days of learning, interaction and hands-on activities focused on taking scientific ideas towards entrepreneurship.

The workshop also featured hands-on exercises, founder interactions, investor perspectives, mentoring clinics and networking opportunities, giving participants a practical understanding of the entrepreneurial journey.

A big thank you to all the participants, speakers, mentors, founders, organisers and partners who made the City Camp a success!

Can cities become the farms of the future?

In this article, Dr. Arpit Shukla, Incubation Manager, VentureStudio Bio-NEST, explores the promise and limitations of urban farming.

From rooftops, basements, and warehouses to hydroponics, aeroponics, and controlled environment agriculture, urban farming is often presented as the future of food. But is it truly a scalable solution, or sometimes just a sustainability theatre?

Dr. Shukla offers a grounded perspective on where urban farming works, where it falls short, and why its real value may lie in climate-conscious, resource-efficient, and resilient city-building.
